column4: The wording كَلَّا بَلْ تُكَذِّبُونَ بِٱلدِّينِ repeats the section's charge almost exactly: the coming settlement itself is denied.
مَٰلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ names the owner of the day on which the section's open account is finally settled.
God will يُوَفِّيهِمُ ٱللَّهُ دِينَهُمُ ٱلْحَقَّ, fully paying people their true due; this is dīn in the section's concrete sense of recompense and payment.
وَكُنَّا نُكَذِّبُ بِيَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ gives the same denial, now confessed by those whose neglected prayer and feeding of the poor are itemized in 74:43-44.
ٱلَّذِينَ يُكَذِّبُونَ بِيَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ directly identifies denial of the settlement day, after 83:1-6 has staged dishonest human accounts.
فَمَا يُكَذِّبُكَ بَعْدُ بِٱلدِّينِ joins the section's verb of denial to dīn as the recompense still awaiting the human being.
Those who يُصَدِّقُونَ بِيَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ affirm the very account denied in 107:1, completing the explicit Meʿārij reversal developed in the source.
إِنَّ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعًا introduces the grasping human type whose specific reaction to received good is withholding in 70:21.
وَإِذَا مَسَّهُ ٱلْخَيْرُ مَنُوعًا depicts the withholding disposition named by يَمْنَعُونَ in 107:7.
A حَقٌّ مَّعْلُومٌ in their wealth reverses the section's unpaid entry: assistance is recognized as a determinate right rather than optional largesse.
لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ identifies the two claimants whose known right is entered in 70:24, opposing the poor person's erased share in the source scene.
إِلَّا ٱلْمُصَلِّينَ opens the exception to the withholding human of 70:21, reversing the source's condemned worshippers.
Their persistence in prayer supplies the precise opposite of prayer that is neglected while its social due is withheld.
لَا يُؤْتُونَ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ and denial of the hereafter place nonpayment of the due and rejection of the final account in the same description.
The commanded declaration “I am only a human like you” ends in woe to the associators, identifying the addressees whom 41:7 then describes as withholding zakāt and denying the hereafter.
وَءَاتِ ذَا ٱلْقُرْبَىٰ حَقَّهُۥ وَٱلْمِسْكِينَ commands payment of the needy person's haqq, the opposite of removing that claim from the section's ledger.
A حَقٌّ لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ in the righteous person's wealth makes the poor person's claim a booked right rather than a favor that may be withheld.
Sincere dīn, prayer, and zakāt are one commanded order here; ذَٰلِكَ دِينُ ٱلْقَيِّمَةِ makes explicit the obedience in which the source's first and last objects meet.
When told to spend, the disbelievers refuse to feed those whom God could feed; their theological objection turns withholding food into denial, just as the source connects the two acts.
وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ is the direct parallel to the source's unmentioned poor person's food-share.
Failure to believe in God is the first count immediately before failure to urge feeding the poor in 69:34, reproducing the source's bond between denial and an unpaid social due.
بَل لَّا تُكْرِمُونَ ٱلْيَتِيمَ makes dishonoring the orphan a charge in the same account opened by the rejected orphan in the source.
وَلَا تَحَٰٓضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ directly repeats the failure to urge provision of the poor person's food.
وَتَأْكُلُونَ ٱلتُّرَاثَ أَكْلًا لَّمًّا exposes indiscriminate consumption of inheritance, the taking of another's booked right behind the preceding neglect of orphan and poor.
Intense love of wealth names the attachment that binds the passage's dishonored orphan, unfed poor person, and consumed inheritance.
لَمْ نَكُ مِنَ ٱلْمُصَلِّينَ is the first confessed unpaid item leading to denial of the Day of Recompense in 74:46.
لَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ ٱلْمِسْكِينَ adds the poor person's unpaid share to the same confession that ends with 74:46's denial of dīn.
كُلُّ نَفْسٍۭ بِمَا كَسَبَتْ رَهِينَةٌ makes each soul collateral for its earnings, turning the section's debt image literal before the reckoning in 74:43-46.
كُلُّ ٱمْرِئٍۭ بِمَا كَسَبَ رَهِينٌ repeats the debt image: each person stands pledged as security for what was earned.
Woe to the defrauders introduces a human account in which one party falsifies what is due, closely matching the source's ledger of denied rights.
The defrauders take their own measure in full, displaying the creditor's demand for exact payment while refusing reciprocity.
When they owe measure or weight to others they cause loss, the same movement from denying the final account to withholding even a small human due.
أَلَا يَظُنُّ أُولَٰٓئِكَ أَنَّهُم مَّبْعُوثُونَ asks whether dishonest account-keepers expect resurrection, explicitly joining the two ledgers.
The “mighty day” is the due date that the defrauders' ordinary transactions should have made perceptible.
The people standing before the Lord of the worlds completes the transfer from a cheated measure to the final audit.
The debt ayah orders a fixed-term دَيْن to be written accurately, dictated by the liable party without diminishing anything, with witnesses: it is the section's two-sided ledger scene in full.
When no scribe is available, a رِهَٰنٌۭ مَّقْبُوضَةٌ secures the debt, while the entrusted party must discharge the trust and testimony must not be hidden.
Immediately before the written-debt ayah, every soul is returned to God and paid in full for what it earned without injustice, joining the earthly ledger to its final closure.
A debtor in hardship receives delay, and remitting the debt as charity is better; the ayah sets mercy within, rather than outside, the creditor-debtor account.
Repentant creditors retain only their principal: لَا تَظْلِمُونَ وَلَا تُظْلَمُونَ defines settlement as neither taking another's right nor losing one's own.
Inheritance is distributed only after a bequest and دَيْن; an outstanding human debt remains a prior claim even at death.
Repeated “after bequest or debt” clauses, together with the ban on injuring heirs, show a ledger of enforceable claims whose settlement precedes distribution.
The placed book omits neither small nor great but enumerates it, and people find their deeds present: even the section's cheapest unpaid due remains on the ledger.
وَكُلُّ شَىْءٍۢ فَعَلُوهُ فِى ٱلزُّبُرِ locates every act in written records, matching the source's account book rather than a forgotten favor.
وَكُلُّ صَغِيرٍۢ وَكَبِيرٍۢ مُّسْتَطَرٌ makes explicit that the small as well as the great is inscribed, illuminating the withheld “small aid.”
Each community kneels and is called to its book to be recompensed for what it did, staging the public opening and settlement of the account.
The divine book speaks truth because deeds were being transcribed, supplying the writing behind the summons in 45:28.
A book with God speaks truth and no one is wronged, making the record both complete and judicially exact.
God writes what people send ahead and the traces they leave, enumerating everything in a clear register; the account retains both act and consequence.
The two receivers seated at right and left record the human being, supplying the scribes for the final ledger.
No word is uttered without a ready observer, so even the spoken denial belongs to the written account.
وَإِنَّ عَلَيْكُمْ لَحَٰفِظِينَ answers the denial of dīn in 82:9 with guardians over the deniers' still-open account.
كِرَامًا كَٰتِبِينَ identifies the guardians as writers, making the record behind the section's ledger explicit.
The writers know what people do, so denial cannot remove an act or withheld right from the account.
The wicked person's register is in Sijjīn, placing the dishonest accounting of 83:1-6 inside a larger written account.
كِتَٰبٌ مَّرْقُومٌ identifies that register as an inscribed book.
The righteous person's register in ʿIlliyyūn supplies the other side of the same final ledger.
كِتَٰبٌ مَّرْقُومٌ again names an inscribed book, now recording the opposite outcome.
Those brought near witness the righteous register, contrasting an attested account with the denier's attempt to erase liability.
God has enumerated all their deeds though they forgot them, so human forgetfulness cannot close or alter the ledger.
وَكُلَّ شَىْءٍ أَحْصَيْنَٰهُ كِتَٰبًا states that everything has been counted in a written record.
When the scrolls are spread open, the account that remained hidden during earthly exchange becomes publicly readable.
Those who deny the Hour are answered that not an atom, nor anything smaller or greater, escapes God and all is in a clear book; denial cannot erase the smallest entry.
No expenditure, “small or great,” is made without being written to their credit for recompense, a direct positive version of the source's smallest unpaid due.
An atom's weight of good will be seen, establishing that no useful gift is too small to enter the final account.
An atom's weight of evil will be seen, so withholding a seemingly trivial aid is not beneath the reckoning.
Just scales are set for resurrection; even a mustard-seed weight is brought, and God suffices as reckoner, combining minute entry and exact settlement.
Each person's deeds are fastened to them and brought out on resurrection as an opened book, making the account inseparable from its debtor.
“Read your book; yourself suffices today as reckoner against you” makes the denier confront and calculate the ledger personally.
Even a mustard-seed weight hidden in rock, heaven, or earth is brought by God, so neither concealment nor smallness cancels a due entry.
God does not wrong even an atom's weight and multiplies a good deed, combining exact non-loss with generosity beyond the balance.
The person given the book in the right hand invites others to read it, the favorable opening of the same final ledger.
إِنِّى ظَنَنتُ أَنِّى مُلَٰقٍ حِسَابِيَهْ names the expectation of meeting one's account, the stance opposed to denying dīn.
The person given the book in the left hand wishes it had not been delivered, staging the debtor's failed attempt to avoid the record.
وَلَمْ أَدْرِ مَا حِسَابِيَهْ expresses dread of learning the account after the book has been handed over.
مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّى مَالِيَهْ shows that accumulated wealth cannot discharge the final liability, even though withheld wealth helped create it.
The weighing that day is true, and heavy scales mark success; the account is an exact adjudication rather than an impression.
Light scales disclose self-inflicted loss through rejected signs, linking denial to a deficit in the final balance.
Heavy scales introduce the favorable side of the final balance sheet.
Light scales introduce its losing side, where neglected small deeds have not disappeared.
A “good loan” to God is multiplied many times; voluntary giving is pictured as a debt whose supreme payer never withholds repayment.
مَّن ذَا ٱلَّذِى يُقْرِضُ ٱللَّهَ قَرْضًا حَسَنًا promises multiplication and a noble wage, reversing the source's default on a small due.
Men and women who give charity are described as lending God a good loan which is multiplied, explicitly joining gift, debt, and recompense.
A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, so an apparent gift to another becomes a credit in the divine account.
Prayer, zakāt, and a good loan to God are commanded together, and whatever people send ahead they find with God as better and greater in reward.
The covenant combines prayer, zakāt, loyal obedience, and a good loan to God, assembling the same duties that the source's denier pulls apart.
The source's dictionary form كذب عليكم الحج means that pilgrimage “became due”; here وَلِلَّهِ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ حِجُّ ٱلْبَيْتِ states that very pilgrimage obligation, then names refusal as disbelief.
God “purchases” believers' lives and wealth for the Garden under a true promise, asking who better fulfills a covenant; obedience is cast as an exchange whose price will be paid.
The alms shares for the poor, needy, debtors, and other recipients are فَرِيضَةً مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ, making the gift an assigned due rather than dispensable kindness.
Righteous dīn is made concrete by giving cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy and traveler, establishing prayer and zakāt, and fulfilling covenants.
Believers are told to spend from divine provision before a day with no bargaining, friendship, or intercession; the opportunity to pay the social due has a closing date.
Givers must not select defective goods that they themselves would accept only with closed eyes, defining a real payment rather than token disposal.
Whatever good people spend is for themselves and يُوَفَّ إِلَيْكُمْ in full without wrong, turning charity into a precisely repaid credit.
Prayer and zakāt are followed by the promise that whatever good people send ahead they will find with God, treating the paid social due as stored credit.
Faith, good works, prayer, and zakāt receive their wage with the Lord, joining obedience and material payment to recompense.
Those who recite, pray, and spend secretly and openly hope for a trade that will never perish, casting worship and giving as one sound account.
God pays their wages in full and adds from bounty, completing the nonperishing transaction of 35:29.
Disbelief, lazy prayer, and unwilling expenditure are given together as the reason contributions are rejected, closely reproducing the source surah's linked failures.
Those who spend to be seen by people while disbelieving in God and the Last Day join ostensible giving, display, and denial in one act.
Charity is nullified by reproach, injury, and spending to be seen while disbelieving in God and the Last Day; a visible payment can therefore be absent from the true account.
The hypocrites rise to prayer lazily and only to be seen, supplying the worship posture that can coexist with a false social account.
Some covenant that if God gives bounty they will give charity and become righteous, establishing a promised payment from a received gift.
When the bounty arrives, they become stingy and turn away, defaulting on the promise recorded in 9:75.
Their broken promise and lying leave hypocrisy in their hearts until the meeting with God, carrying the unpaid covenant into its due date.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's way are warned of painful punishment, treating retained wealth as an outstanding liability.
The hoard is heated and used to brand its owners, and they are told to taste what they stored, a material settlement of the withholding named in 9:34.
The stingy, those who command stinginess, and those who conceal God's bounty display the same refusal to pass received benefit onward.
Those stingy with God's bounty should not call it good; what they withheld will be hung around their necks on resurrection, turning retention into a collectible liability.
People are invited to spend, but whoever is stingy is stingy only against the self; God is rich and they are poor, reversing their imagined creditor position.
Those who are stingy and command others to stinginess reproduce the communal refusal of aid, while God's self-sufficiency shows who truly owns the account.
People are told to spend from what God has made them successors over, so the wealth from which aid is withheld is itself held on trust.
The question “why do you not spend?” is answered by God's ultimate inheritance of heaven and earth, exposing withholding as a temporary holder's refusal.
مَنَّاعٍۢ لِّلْخَيْرِ names a habitual preventer of good, the direct moral posture carried by يَمْنَعُونَ in the source.
مَّنَّاعٍۢ لِّلْخَيْرِ describes the obstinate doubter as one who keeps good back, joining withheld benefit to uncertainty about the final truth.
The hypocrites command that support be withheld from those with the Messenger until they disperse, while the treasuries actually belong to God.
Wealth and children must not distract from remembrance, since possession becomes loss when it obscures the account owed to God.
“Spend from what We provided you” before death prevents the futile plea for delay in order to give charity once the payment period has closed.
People of means must not swear to stop giving relatives, the needy, and emigrants; the verse directly interrupts a chosen withholding of material aid.
Orphans must receive their property, and guardians must not substitute bad for good or consume it, making the orphan's claim an enforceable entry.
Guardians test orphans, deliver their property at maturity, avoid waste, and call witnesses; وَكَفَىٰ بِٱللَّهِ حَسِيبًا places the transfer under divine audit.
Consuming orphan property unjustly is described as eating fire, the final charge attached to the right that was taken rather than acknowledged.
The ruling demands justice for orphans and addresses withheld prescribed shares, directly reopening the orphan's erased line in the source ledger.
The orphan's property, full measure and weight, and just speech appear together, joining protected right and accurate accounting.
The orphan's property may be approached only in the best manner, and covenants are answerable, combining a vulnerable claimant with an obligation that will be asked about.
فَأَمَّا ٱلْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ commands the opposite of driving the orphan away.
وَأَمَّا ٱلسَّآئِلَ فَلَا تَنْهَرْ forbids repelling the petitioner, the interpersonal gesture that begins the withholding of even minor help.
The righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive despite their own love of the food, paying precisely the human claims neglected in the source.
They seek neither جَزَآءً nor thanks from recipients; the gift creates no human debt even though it remains in God's account.
Fear of a grim day explains the unrequited giving in 76:8-9, opposing denial of the day that licenses withholding.
Freeing a neck is the first concrete payment on the steep path, replacing possessive power with release.
Feeding on a day of hunger reverses refusal to make the poor person's food available.
The orphan of near kin identifies one beneficiary of that costly feeding.
The destitute person in misery identifies the other beneficiary, completing the scene opposed to denied small assistance.
The relative, needy person, and traveler are each to receive their haqq; seeking God's face turns payment of their claim into worship.
وَءَاتُوا۟ حَقَّهُۥ يَوْمَ حَصَادِهِ requires the produce's due on harvest day, making provision carry another's payable right at the moment it arrives.
The restrained poor are mistaken for self-sufficient because they do not beg insistently; this identifies the hidden creditor whose share must not depend on asking.
Those who prefer others despite their own need and are saved from the soul's stinginess embody the opposite direction from withholding al-māʿūn.
Spending what one can and being protected from the soul's stinginess prepares the “good loan” of 64:17 and reverses the source's refusal.
Rendering trusts to their owners and judging justly gives the positive rule for recognizing another's haqq instead of taking it away.
وَلَا تَبْخَسُوا۟ ٱلنَّاسَ أَشْيَآءَهُمْ forbids diminishing what belongs to people, the commercial form of erasing a claimant's line from the ledger.
Full measure and just weight are coupled with not depriving people of their things, making accurate accounting a social obligation.
Shuʿayb's command to give full measure and weight and not diminish people's goods restates the same two-party justice.
The one who is stingy and considers himself self-sufficient supplies the inner posture of the person who refuses minor aid.
وَكَذَّبَ بِٱلْحُسْنَىٰ couples that stinginess with denial of the promised best outcome, echoing denial as the warrant for nonpayment.
وَمَا يُغْنِى عَنْهُۥ مَالُهُۥٓ إِذَا تَرَدَّىٰ shows that the retained wealth cannot meet the final deficit it helped produce.
The one who gives and is mindful opens the exact opposite course from stinginess and withheld aid.
Believing in the best promise makes giving in 92:5 the positive counterpart of denial in 92:9.
God's promised ease answers the giver's affirmation, while 92:10 gives the denier the reverse path.
The most mindful person gives wealth to purify himself, directly reversing the withholding and self-sufficiency of 92:8.
No one has a favor with him to be repaid; the giver discharges human reciprocity and seeks recompense only from God.
The hoarder جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ counts wealth while ignoring the account in which that wealth and its uses will be counted.
Thinking wealth makes him immortal exposes why his private tally displaces the closing day of the true ledger.
Divorced women receive a fair provision حَقًّا عَلَى ٱلْمُتَّقِينَ, making a material kindness an owed right.
A divorced woman is to receive a fair gift according to the giver's means, حَقًّا عَلَى ٱلْمُحْسِنِينَ; ability affects amount, not the obligation to give.
The bequest for parents and relatives is described as a prescribed fair duty, another human claim entered before an estate closes.
هَٰذَا عَطَآؤُنَا فَٱمْنُنْ أَوْ أَمْسِكْ بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ combines gift, giving or holding back, and “without account,” marking sovereign largesse as a boundary to human default on a right.
God extends عَطَآءِ رَبِّكَ to both groups and His gift is not restricted, opposing the human impulse to obstruct benefit.
The question who could provide if God withheld His provision reverses scale: the person withholding a small benefit lives wholly on an unwithheld gift.
جَزَآءً مِّن رَّبِّكَ عَطَآءً حِسَابًا places recompense, gift, and measured sufficiency in a single phrase, the same semantic meeting developed between dīn and māʿūn.
God's dīn is set beside all in heaven and earth having أَسْلَمَ to Him willingly or unwillingly and returning to Him, making submission and final return the root beneath the account.
The best dīn belongs to one who أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُۥ لِلَّهِ while doing good, directly realizing the source dictionary's sense of obedient submission.
وَلَهُ ٱلدِّينُ وَاصِبًا assigns enduring dīn to God alone, supporting the source's “obedience” sense rather than only the name of a future day.
Worship with dīn made sincere for God presents religion as undivided obedience owed to its sole recipient.
أَلَا لِلَّهِ ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْخَالِصُ states that pure dīn belongs to God, while false patrons expose diverted obedience.
Ibrahim answers the command “submit” with أَسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ, enacting the yieldedness identified as dīn's underlying root sense in the source.
Ibrahim and Jacob charge their children to die only as submitters because God chose the dīn for them, explicitly joining dīn to islām.
A straight dīn and the creed of Ibrahim name the ordered way whose obedience is unfolded in the next two ayat.
Prayer, sacrifice, life, and death are all for God, showing how the dīn of 6:161 claims the whole account rather than a verbal affiliation.
“No partner,” “I was commanded,” and being first of the submitters complete the obedience implicit in the section's root definition.
Being named Muslims is followed by prayer, zakāt, and holding fast to God, bringing submission, worship, and the paid social due together.
Prayer, zakāt, and obedience to the messenger form one command, making māʿūn's dictionary senses of obedience and zakāt converge in practice.
Prayer and zakāt are joined to certainty in the hereafter, the positive threefold relation opposed by negligent worship, withheld aid, and denial.
Prayer and zakāt again accompany certainty in the hereafter, linking payment of the present due to confidence in the final account.
Commerce does not distract these people from remembrance, prayer, and zakāt because they fear a day when hearts and eyes overturn; ordinary trade remains under the final audit.
God repays them for the best of their deeds and adds from bounty, while providing without account, completing the commercial and eschatological scene of 24:37.
Usury meant to increase through people's wealth does not increase with God, whereas zakāt seeking His face is multiplied, correcting a false and a true account of gain.
After the waived requirement of pre-consultation charity, prayer, zakāt, and obedience remain due, clarifying mercy about one payment without canceling submission.
The ayah places dīn al-ḥaqq beside payment of jizyah and being brought low; whatever its legal context, it concretely joins a material due to dīn's submission sense developed in the source.
لَآ إِكْرَاهَ فِى ٱلدِّينِ is a necessary boundary on the source dictionary's “submission” sense: dīn is not produced by human compulsion.
The question what deceived the human being concerning the “generous Lord” names the giver whose bounty is answered by denial of dīn in 82:9.
Creation, proportioning, and balancing begin to itemize the generous Lord's prior gifts before the denial charged in 82:9.
Composition in whatever form God willed completes the received-benefit side of the account that the human then denies.
The wicked enter the fire يَوْمَ ٱلدِّينِ, giving the denied day its concrete settlement.
They cannot be absent from the fire, so the liable party cannot evade the due date named in 82:15.
وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ magnifies the day whose reality the deniers try to remove from their account.
The repeated question about the Day of Recompense prolongs the confrontation with the denied settlement.
No soul controls anything for another and command belongs to God that day, identifying the sole authority who closes every account.
The raised deniers cry هَٰذَا يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ, recognizing the due day only when settlement begins.
“This is the day of separation which you used to deny” explains the recognition in 37:20 and turns prior denial into present judgment.
Ibrahim hopes for forgiveness of his error يَوْمَ ٱلدِّينِ, showing that the final settlement also admits the creditor's mercy.
Receiving the book in the right hand begins the favorable settlement of the written account.
فَسَوْفَ يُحَاسَبُ حِسَابًا يَسِيرًا promises an easy reckoning, showing that account need not mean denial of mercy.
Receiving the book behind one's back gives the opposite disposition of the same recorded liabilities.
The recipient calls for destruction when the unfavorable account is opened.
Entering the blaze is the settlement attached to that book.
إِنَّ إِلَيْنَآ إِيَابَهُمْ locates everyone's return with the owner of the account.
ثُمَّ إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا حِسَابَهُم makes their accounting God's own charge, directly stating who closes the ledger.
Those who fulfill what God commands to be joined and fear a bad account combine honored obligations with awareness of audit.
Those who do not answer their Lord would offer every earthly possession as ransom, yet theirs is the bad account; retained wealth cannot buy release.
The mockers demand their allotted share before the Day of Account, using the language of a payable portion while denying its appointed time.
Severe punishment follows forgetting the Day of Account, showing that practical misrule grows from treating the audit as absent.
Moses seeks refuge from every arrogant person who does not believe in the Day of Account, tying refusal of judgment to oppressive power.
